title: Spinal subarachnoid hemorrhage progressing to spinal cord compression in a patient on a direct oral anticoagulant: a case report
case_prompt: An 82-year-old woman presented with sudden onset radiating chest and epigastric pain extending to both the upper and lower back. Her medical history included atrial fibrillation managed with apixaban, ischemic heart disease, hypertension, osteoporosis, and a pacemaker implanted eight months earlier. On initial evaluation, she was hypertensive at 189/72 mmHg and had respiratory alkalosis; other cardiac workup and physical examination were unremarkable. A few hours after arrival, she developed new bilateral lower extremity weakness, sensory changes, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a positive Babinski reflex. Noncontrast head CT showed fluid–blood levels in the occipital horns of the lateral ventricles, subarachnoid blood in the left posterior fossa, and peripheral hyperdensity at the craniocervical junction suggestive of peri-mesencephalic subarachnoid hemorrhage.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Aortic dissection was suspected given chest pain and neurological signs — “Due to worsening neurological symptoms and chest pain, a CT angiography (CTA) of the neck, chest and abdomen was done, to rule out an aortic dissection.”  
2. Intracranial aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation was considered as the source of SAH — “No vascular abnormalities were observed on concurrent CTA…”  
3. Tumor or other mass lesion in the spine was investigated as a cause of hemorrhage — “No etiological factor was identified in neither of the scans.”  
4. Spinal epidural hematoma was a key differential in an anticoagulated patient, but imaging localized the hematoma intradurally — “Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed SSH hemorrhage with significant cord compression in the thoracic regions T6–T9.”  
5. Subarachnoid rather than subdural or epidural location was confirmed at surgery — “A dorsally located subarachnoid hematoma at T6–T9 level was evacuated.”
